Our companies lawyer regularly stopped by in Tommy Bahama shirts and khaki shorts when he would visit for strategy meeting with the CEO, COO, CCO, and the CFO. If he showed up to something dressed up you knew that there were some serious dealings going on (those dealings were usually reserved for meetings out of the office). People were more freaked out when they saw people dressed up because there is no reason one needs to code, design, project manage in corporate attire. Engineers of both sexes in shorts and a tshirt during the summer is the norm….its really no big deal. My CFO used to be in banking for medical offices prior to coming to tech and he told me he kept a dress shirt and jacket in his old office in case he needed to be pulled into meetings but otherwise stayed in a T-shirt or polo since he did 90% of his work managing accounts from a computer in his office with a closed door. I can appreciate the hypothetical value of some emphasis words when texting, as they may compensate for the absence of tone and facial expression in this mode of communication. For example, if I propose something via text message and the person responds "okay", I am left wondering if they are giving passive assent or whether they are enthusiastically onboard. Even the response, "Yeah" instead of "Yes" could be an alternate spelling with the same meaning or it could be sardonic (as in "Yeah, right" said in a mocking tone).

Email and texting can be a great convenience but they can also complicate communication greatly when used for important matters.

"Are you paying in cash or card?"  "Card." "Okay, perfect. Tap or insert when you're ready."  "Do you want the salad or fries that comes with that?" "I'll have the fries." "Perfect. And anything to drink?""A lemonade." [While writing] "Perrrfecttt."  "What's your date a birth?" [I give my date of birth.] "Perfect. And what are we seeing you for today?" And so on, ad nauseum. It's not a huge corruption of language, but it just seems a little silly for the context. Gee, I'm so glad I got all those answers not just right, but "perfect."  I'm a superstar at giving answers!  The perfection oozes off me. (What's worse is that I've even caught myself using it a few times. . . ugh, not perfect. )

On the other hand, the "romance" languages, deriving from Roman Latin, are supposed to be more passionate and elaborate. The expression "Spanish is the loving tongue" illustrates that.

In the song by Butch Hancock, the speaker expresses his love lament for a lady he once desired in "old Mexico": "Her favorite poets all agree/Spanish is a lovin' tongue/But she never spoke Spanish to me."

comments.name: jchicago
comments.body: The use of the word "right" after a person said something is more insidious than a mere accent on the predicate statement.  It is a rhetorical device that asserts that the other person agrees with you and is often delivered mid-phrase so as to escape contradiction.  To contest it, the listener is forced to stop the flow and say, "No, not right", which most people won't do.  It startles people when you threaten to contradict their subtle attempt to force your thinking into alignment with theirs.

As a physician let me tell you that if _anyone_ thinks it's easy to simply "get help" for a mentally ill teenager or adult, they have never had the experience of being responsibile for someone who has paranoid delusions and does not want treatment. There are no laws mandating treatment. There are no long term beds for the mentally ill. 

Obviously guns should not be in the hands of people who are mentally unstable. But our laws give them the right to as many guns as they can carry. There was nothing the boy's father did that was illegal, so it would have been hard for him to know it was wrong.

The story doesn't tell us what the boy's father believes now about the right for anyone to carry a gun with no requirement to prove one is stable enough to do so safely. Maybe he has come to his senses and realizes that the laws we have now are insane.

comments.name: Alex
comments.body:
It is reasonable to hold people accountable for giving a person with obvious mental health issues a gun.

But holding parents responsible for the actions of teenage children with serious mental health issues is likely a mistake.  Parents, obviously, do not choose to have children with mental health issues. In some cases, criminal behavior by teenage children is a result of bad upbringing, such as broken families or parents addicted to drugs or alcohol.

But in most cases, serious mental illness is due to biology, and factors medicine does not understand.  In most cases, we cannot and should not hold parents responsible.

Society does not provide parents with the tools they need. Long term involuntary confinement is usually not possible, even for minors.  It's not at all clear that pyschiatric care could have helped Colt, mental illness is difficult to treat.

Giving his son access to a gun was a criminal offense. If the strong punishment was levied for that offense,  then it qualifies as justice.  If the lengthy jail sentence was levied for failing to manage his son's mental illness, I'm not at all sure this is justice.

The Second Amendment reads "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed." Like many, I would like to see the first phrase reflected in SCOTUS rulings and our laws.  Individuals with mental illness and for the most part minors should not have firearms.

But it makes no sense that the Iran would target Minnesota and then stop there.  

First of all a massive attack on any American water supply company or reservoirs would bring about an emergency reaction from the federal government as well as state and local management of the water supplies.  And, if it was an attack by an external enemy on the system we'd uncover who did it and where it came from far more rapidly than this so-called attack was handled. 
 
This attack seems more like home-grown trouble makers rather than Iran or any other nation interested in causing real havoc.  
I believe that if Iran really did sponsor or direct an attack on America water supply that the attack would be catastrophic and the response more catastrophic than Iran can imagine.
  
That doesn't mean  we should let our guard down and not take any precautions.  This is a warning.  Water, electric, and food are the 3 most fundament infrastructure elements of American society.   We can't live or survive without those critical resources.  

So, this wasn't Pearl Harbor or even the World Trade Center attack of 1993.  But it is a warning to be more vigilant and far more greatly prepared.   Oh, wait. Trump dismantled FEMA.

comments.name: Devout Skeptic

The concept of an education in liberal arts has much value, but we need to remember that it's based on classical Greek concepts of who should be educated and how.

The *liberal arts* were for free (liberal) citizens who had leisure to debate philosophy and devote their time to civic enterprises. In contrast, the *servile arts* were for people who had to work for a living. The potter, the master glassblower, and the sommelier each practice a servile art. The servile arts were considered inherently inferior to the liberal arts, precisely because they had practical uses.

We are now able to see the value of "practical" learning in a liberal education. Finding and fixing a malfunction in a computer program or an internal combustion engine involves a thought process just as rigorous as philosophical argument or rhetorical debate... but it's a rather different thought process. It's one that comes with a built-in pass/fail test: either the program or engine runs when you're done, or it doesn't.

Without exposure to this type of thought, I would argue, a *modern* liberal arts education is incomplete.

People heavily invested index funds, especially people nearing or in retirement, need to understand what the AI risk means to them and how to reduce the risk if they wish to do that. Because so much of the S&P 500 market cap is tied up in AI tech giants and other high-risk stocks like Tesla and SpaceX, the downside of a crash for index fund investors might be much worse than even the 2008 banking meltdown and its aftermath.

One way to reduce the risk is modified index funds offered by some companies that let the investor own the S&P 500 minus high-risk tech giants. Another way is to buy index funds limited to stocks that pay dividends (the tech giants mostly do not). In both cases, there is a potential cost to reducing risk -- you may also reduce your return significantly if the AI economic boom comes to pass. 

As a retired person, I'm willing to give up a few points of return in exchange for not losing sleep over a potential tech stock crash. I saw the late 1990s crash of tech stocks at close range and it was not pretty.

comments.body:
Just be careful of what the active sweetener is in these products (the best are Allulose and Monk Fruit). The common ones on labels today are:

Maltitol — dominant in mainstream sugar-free chocolate and hard candy (Russell Stover, Hershey's sugar-free). Tastes and behaves most like sugar, but it's ~75% as sweet and has a real glycemic impact (GI ~35).
Erythritol — the workhorse in "keto" candy, usually blended with stevia or monk fruit. Near-zero calories, ~70% as sweet, mostly absorbed and excreted in urine rather than fermented in the gut.
Xylitol — chewing gum, mints, some chocolate. Sugar-sweet, ~2.4 cal/g. Fatally toxic to dogs.
Sorbitol — older sugar-free gums and mints, also a laxative ingredient (that's the tell).
Isomalt — hard candies and lozenges; holds up to heat well.
Allulose — technically a rare sugar, not a sugar alcohol, but it's replacing them fast in newer brands because it doesn't ferment in the colon.

The downsides

GI distress is the main one, and it's dose-dependent. Most sugar alcohols aren't fully absorbed in the small intestine, so they draw water into the gut (osmotic diarrhea) and get fermented by colon bacteria (gas, bloating, cramping). Maltitol and sorbitol are the worst offenders — roughly 20–50g can trigger symptoms, which is about half a bag of sugar-free gummy bears.

comments.name: Cindy
comments.body:
This article seems to be focused on professional white-collar jobs, and I don't doubt that there's a high status/low status sorting going on and that women are getting the low status end of that stick.  What I'm curious about is, what is happening to the men who are not getting those high status jobs?  Presumably there are fewer of those jobs and they require more education, and men aren't attending college and graduating as often as women are so they wouldn't be qualified for them.  Given that the male/female ratio in the U.S. is roughly 50/50, it means that the number of men is greater than the number of high status jobs available to them.  So what are they doing?  Are they mostly in the trades, are they playing video games in their parents' basement, or what?

I'd like to see an overall picture of how women are doing compared to men.  Are they actually better off even if their jobs aren't considered as prestigious?

comments.name: Joan
comments.body: I have seen this in my own industry.Reading the analysis here is profound. I experienced the rise of the woman's movement back in the early 70's and the effects on my industry - the film and television business and it's sister, commercial advertising. Television was the first to recognize hire a handful of female directors, At the same time in advertising, women were beginning to emerge as producers. I became a script supervisor, a position that put me in  position that could influence  decision making on the set. In television, directors are hired hands, just like the rest of the crew. The real power is the show runners and the writers. In advertising, the creative control has been passed on from the producer to the art director, and in film industry, script supervisor have been cut out of film prep phase almost entirely. Looking through the smoke and mirrors you'll notice the glass ceiling is firmly in place.to this day the film industry and the music industry have very few women that have progressed. Way back in the mid 70's, I remember thinking the insurance companies were more accepting of women in leadership positions than the industries that promoted creativity. To this day that hasn't changed.

Technology is a tool. The same way a hammer or a screwdriver are. It’s all about how you choose to use it. And the boundaries you set. I think the reason a lot of people have let it take over their lives is that they don’t know how to set boundaries, know when to put it away, when to look and when it’s just a distraction more important real world interactions. You don’t need to post everything about yourself nor do you have to follow other people’s feeds. 

I work from home though I could go into an office but given all of my colleagues are spread around the globe, I appreciate having the flexibility and I enjoy seeing with them online for calls. As my parents got older, I did install ring cameras, for their safety and my peace of mind. None of us compulsively check the videos unless there is a reason to;  usually is to watch the wildlife like local deer. I don’t do social media and  make a point of having friends in real life.

As the administration rolls back drinking water standards for several PFAS compounds, it's also worth asking why fluorinated pharmaceuticals have received comparatively little public scrutiny. That observation is especially thought provoking in light of recent peer-reviewed pharmaceutical toxicology research proposing a mechanistic link involving persistent organofluorine toxicity. comments.name: Elizabeth Brannan

So many things are awful about these buses: 1) They should have been designed with a “first in, first out” plan, i.e. the first passengers to board would be the first passengers to exit. Since they weren’t designed that way, the first passengers to board crowd around the doors trying to get a good spot for exiting. 2) This crowding at the doors blocks access to the rest of the bus, whereupon bus conductors yell rudely at people, ordering them to move back —in English only. Non-English speakers are at a loss to understand the maddening system.
3) The buses don’t depart until they are full. Sorry to sound elitist, but this means that first and business class passengers must wait until the entire plane (or at least a broad percentage of it) has boarded. Sometimes they even have to wait for the crew. And throughout the endless wait, they are being mauled by people trying to get pas them with their carry-ons (because the aisles are too narrow for the roll-aboards) and are being yelled at by the conductors. Inevitably, therefore, they are the last to arrive at Immigration, where long lines have already formed.
         In my view, Dulles is the worst airport in the US.

-

comments.name: JSD
comments.body:
I will bet anyone dollars-to-donuts that the AI sneaking-out incident was engineered or at the very least parameters were knowingly set to allow for such behavior.  

First, when we say that the AI escaped… that’s not how AI or neural nets work. The AI continued to execute its processes on the same network of computers that it started and stop on. It didn’t somehow replicate itself on some other network outside its ecosystem. What it did was started sending out internet packets in the same way that web browsers or internet-enabled applications do. 

“Escaping” in this context simply means being allowed to communicate with other computers on the internet.  With the ability to start making internet queries, it basically did the equivalent of Google searches to find information on the test it was being tested against and successfully bypassed its security in the same manner a hacker with a set of robust malware would and then used some adaptive routines to find the information it was seeking which it downloaded and used to improve its test score. 

At no point, did the AI ever exist outside its original infrastructure. It did not replicate. It just gathered information from an external network. While this is being eaten up by the techno-enthusiast hype machine and the embarrassingly naive wide-eyed press like the unveiling of a digital superintelligence, really all it shows is the maybe-careless probably-intentional failure to establish a simple digital sandbox.

It would not cause much sky viewing pollution if the arrays were in geosynchronous orbit on the day side of Earth.

comments.name: Harmony?
comments.body:
The fight is between two industrial ecosystems: the traditional automotive industry, built around highly specialized suppliers and decades of optimization for internal combustion engines, and the new, vertically integrated model exemplified by Chinese companies such as BYD (and to large extent, Tesla or Rivian) . In the traditional ecosystem, innovation is distributed across a complex network of suppliers and engineering disciplines. In the integrated model, batteries, software, semiconductors, electronics, manufacturing, and vehicle design evolve together as a single system. As electric vehicles become increasingly defined by software and systems integration rather than mechanical engineering, this model can  innovate faster, reduce costs, and bring new technologies to market more quickly.

The same dynamic is at play in the military sector. Traditional  industries remain organized around large, expensive platforms such as fighter aircraft, tanks, and warships, supported by long procurement cycles and specialized supply chains etc. The war in Ukraine, however, has demonstrated the growing importance of inexpensive drones, autonomous systems, AI, and rapidly evolving software. Rather than simply replacing traditional platforms, these technologies are changing how military capability is developed and deployed. So In both sectors, Car and Defense the real competition is no longer just between products or companies, but between industrial ecosystems.

comments.name: Ela Dominican High, Class of 1970
comments.body: Yuppie. Funny word. I moved to Warsaw, Poland in 1991 and read a Polish daily paper that included a Friday section highlighting weekend events. The night life info described bars frequented by “japiszony” which was a word I’d never seen before and couldn’t find in any dictionary. Then one day it dawned on me that the word “yuppie” had been Polish-ized, converted into Polish phonetic spelling with a Polish twist at the end. The Polish “j” sounds like the English “y.” Yuppie = japi. Quirky hobby, being a word detective. But the Polish word disappeared into obscurity soon enough. Still, there must have been “japiszony” in the immediate post-communist Poland era.

comments.name: Oscar
comments.body: I would argue that the Yuppie era was the beginning of the misery wrought by late stage capitalism. Women were accepted -- grudgingly -- into the office in large numbers. (At my law firm, the receptionist greeted the male lawyers with "good morning, Mr. Smith" and the female lawyers with, "hi, Kim".) The hours were -- and still are -- grueling and inhumane, but we didn't earn anywhere near the 1980s equivalent of the $2M/year that junior partners at top law firms earn now. And without the technology to work from home and close deals remotely, we were physically in the office for 18, 19, 20 hour days, culminating in an all-nighter or two leading into a closing. Is it any wonder that many of us didn't find/make the time to find a partner, get married and have kids (if those ships hadn't sailed) until our late 30s/early 40s? Or that those kids, having watched us continue in these grueling roles in which we barely enjoyed our youth and middle age, want no part of this rat race? I applaud Gen Z's approach to life. Work is a means to an end, and maybe that end doesn't have to include luxury trips to Europe, Hawaii, and the UK, or a BMW, or even fancy clothes. Maybe, just maybe, enjoying your life, albeit in smaller ways, might be more important. If I had it to do over again, I'd be with the "kids".

comments.name: Devon
comments.body:
This article is a dishonest portrait of what transpired, and I hope people take it with a grain of salt. It frames the issue with AI in fandom as having stemmed from a single document, when the problem has a history rooted in plagiarism, Big Name Fan culture, and rampant consumerism. 

It's obvious from reading the first few pages of the document that @heatedrivalryai took issue with the deception from scammers stating they were against the use of generative AI to further their grifts. These "writers" took advantage of a community built historically on, as Prof. Tushnet indicates, low stakes and a love for media. If you did your research, you would have learned that Opal Apparition managed to get a book deal from Wolfbird- which is also AI generated, she admitted to it- and nearly walked away 6-7 figures richer for the scam. Another "author" boosted sales for her original book (suspected to be AI-assisted) from her popular AI-generated fanfiction. 

This is the issue: not the release of the document, but the fact that people lied and benefited from scamming others. Of course the docwriters went after the popular fanfictions, those were the ones that were getting used for material gain!

These grifters received social clout and influence that they weaponized to keep people from talking about AI in fandom at all, at the risk of death threats, harassment, and real-life career impacts, just to hide their tracks. Your silence on these issues in this article reads as disingenuous.

comments.name: Ethan Allen
comments.body:
I can attest to this problem from personal experience.
All property owners in rural areas are under a legal obligation to keep their land clear of brush, including tall grass and scrub, through a regular process of ‘debrousaillage’.  This is intended precisely to eliminate the danger of fires being able to take hold and spread quickly in at areas where there typically aren’t large firefighting resources.  Failure to do this carries a fine that can be imposed by the local mayor.

But in reality, because of a decline in active farming (driven by the long term trend of people leaving the land and moving to towns and cities) this means that more and more rural land is effectively abandoned, and is covered in brush and other combustible vegetation.
Remaining farmers don’t have the luxury of either the time, money, staffing, or sometimes even equipment to carry out the necessary work sufficiently frequently.
And the land owned in the margins by private homeowners (as noted in the article) is a problem because those people don’t have the equipment to do the work, or don’t own the land where the majority of the problem exists.
But just like in the US, municipal authorities need to define a safety zone of cleared land around the margins of any inhabited land, and they have to enforce those clearances both with real fine, or through doing the clearances and billing landowners.

As to the cause of the fires, it seems obvious -- given the 162 arrests (so far) in France -- that arson may have been the main cause. (Similar story in California as well).

The path to avoiding these types of events in the future is clear, but I am pessimistic that anything sensible will happen policy-wise.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
When I lived in a wildfire prone area of California’s Sierra Nevada I made a decision to not harden my house against wildfire.

Why? For several reasons. For one thing I didn’t think it was possible in these days of mega fires with 1,000 foot long flame lengths and embers starting fires a mile away from the main fire.

In addition I’d seen pictures of houses which survived wildfires standing alone in a moonscape of toxic ash.

I decided that if a wildfire destroyed my town I didn’t want to have to continue living in a toxic wasteland, I’d rather take the insurance money and move elsewhere.

comments.name: Carole Smith
comments.body: I grew up in Malibu Ca in the 1970s and 80s. We werent rich- many weren’t then. Anyways every summer all of kids and Dad and Mom spent many days doing back breaking work clearing brush, trimming trees etc. The fire department was VERY strict then. All potential fuel must be removed at least 50 feet surrounding our property, or else they would impose hefty fines daily until we did. Ditto in Topanga Canyon. There were multiple brush fires there over the years. None devastating. I don’t know why, but that practice stopped decades ago. Now the fires are devastating. I hope that practice resumes.

comments.name: Greg
comments.body:
Clearing vegetation around homes is dangerous. Wildfires jump from structure to structure, not from structures to plants to structure. I live in Altadena, California and after our fire, lush gardens surrounded burned out shells of homes. My house survived because it’s surrounded by lush, green vegetation. That’s where the fire stopped.

You can confirm this is easily by taking a blow torch to the plants around your home and then to your home. The house will catch fire quickly while the plants will resist the fire until they’ve been throughly dried out. It takes time and the vegetation gives us time to stop the fire.

comments.name: Marty in Point Loma
comments.body:
This is so similar to the issues facing California and the massive wild fires that occur here.  Brush management is mandatory - but over time enforcement has the same issues.  As development pushes outward towards natural habitat the interface is what creates the potential for catastrophic scenarios.  Look at Pacific Palisades.  The winds were gusting to 90 MPH and the embers going out of the habitat areas that caught fire were blowing 1 mile down wind and catching houses on fire.  

As I have seen in video and photographs - the fires were jumping from house to house .  Not always was it vegetation.  Obviously the fires in France were plant / tree initiated and when having a dense forest that is used as crop production the fuel load is so dense it will explode in hot dry weather

comments.name: Lynda Schuler

I used to live in Pacific Palisades, where blame was thrown at politicians, firefighters, and homeowners themselves.  It's fine to report the facts but we are burning ourselves up, literally.  Climate change is the spark that is lighting these historic fires.  Please, in your coverage, always keep that fact paramount.

My concern is the distinction between  Value Capture vs. Value Creation.

AI will create trillions of dollars in value for humanity (vastly superior products, higher productivity, cheaper services) but AI requires continuous, astronomical spending on data centers, chips (NVIDIA GPUs), and nuclear energy just to keep the lights on . If the cost to run the AI (inference costs) remains high, but competition forces them to give the features away for free, profit margins will compress significantly . The hyperscalers themselves may not capture that value in the form of higher profit margins.  The hyperscalers (META, Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon etc. ) might find themselves trapped in a hyper-competitive loop: delivering absolute sci-fi magic to consumers for pennies, while their own margins are squeezed by the brutal reality of commoditization and massive infrastructure costs.

comments.name: Che Beauchard
comments.body: When I read the headline for this story I assumed--it turned out correctly--that it concerned India.  But thinking about the headline provoked a line of thought about what we mean when we use the word democracy.  Government by the people.  Or perhaps:  rule of the majority.  I remember such definitions from high school civics classes. But that facts on the ground differ.  Government through the coercion of money and propaganda seems closer to experience.  Government through manipulation of those who crave power the most.  Only the gullible can think that India or America--or any of the other countries one might be tempted to call democracies--are governed by the people.  Not when our representative leaders are selected through manipulation by power and money.  Democracy is farce as much as reality.  Was the leader of America ever the leader of the "free world"?  Government of those most motivated to rule others is more like it.  Are some systems worse than others?  Were Nazi Germany or Stalinist USSR worse than Switzerland or Denmark or ...?   Let's assume they were in many ways.  But that doesn't tell us that we've had democracies.  Perhaps democracy is possible only in small groups living isolated in tribal groups, where everyone speaking actually can be heard.  But with millions homeless and voiceless we surely do not have government by the people--majority or minority.

An interesting commentary, but there is a much larger question here than whether to raise rates or to forecast future Fed actions, and that is the composition of the task forces Warsh will use to determine the facts to be used in setting rates and the mathematical models which will be used to analyze those facts in setting rates.

Warsh was asked that question point blank at Wednesday's conference and he reused to answer it and this looms larger for me than the rate decision.

The essence of the question was how could the public have confidence in the Fed's decisions when Marc Andreessen was made co-chair of one of Warsh's task forces, given his political positions and his clear financial conflicts of interest because of his investments in crypto currency and his positions on government regulation of that and the AI industry..

The response was not to answer the question but to redirect the inquiry to different matters. Watch the conference to see Warsh's dodge.

To me, it confirmed the original criticism of Warsh's nomination - namely, that he would serve the President's interests, not the public's.

This is a point on which the Journal needs to dig deeper.

There is more than one way for Trump to undo Fed independence and these task forces with a complicit Warsh would give him just what he wants.

AI models for code development can be trained to leave subtle security flaws in the code they develop.  It is impossible to detect these flaws by examining the weights.  The only way to do it is to build multiple systems, attack them with a tool like Mythos, and see a pattern in the exploits it finds.

AI tools can also be trained to encode secret information steganographically in the unclassified text they produce.  This is effectively undetectable.

Together, this makes Chinese AI systems a critical security hole.  For example, if Hugging Face used the Chinese AI that it used against Open AI's agent to write a report on the incident and published the report it may steganographically encode information about other Hugging Face vulnerabilities.  Those will now be in the hands of the CCP.

The US needs to make sure that we release open weight AIs that are more powerful than the most powerful Chinese open weight AIs and that running them on US data centers is cheaper than running the Chinese AIs on Chinese data centers.

I never thought, even as a child reader, that I had to prefer Ma or Pa.  I found them both fascinating as individuals who each had a necessary role to play in the family.  Ma doesn't need a defense in my eyes, because I always appreciated her.

That said, re-reading the books to my own children yesterday, the pathos of her situation stuck me more forcibly, as described in this piece.  My kids are pretty observant, and they quickly picked up on Ma's catchphrase being, "Oh, Charles!" There's a whole universe in those two words -- love, frustration, resignation, admonishment, and fear.

I feel for Ma.  She catches a lot of flak nowadays for her attitude towards Indians.  Her words are indefensible, but an astute reader can also see that she was genuinely terrified in LHOTP.  And I can't blame her. They were living practically alone on land technically not under US jurisdiction, in a time when violence often erupted between settlers and the indigenous inhabitants.  She couldn't express that fear to Pa or the girls (or tell Pa to get them the hell outta there), so it came out as unbridled racism instead.

Its mission was to boost the US's first space station, SkyLab to a safer orbit when its orbital status degraded due to similar solar activity circumstances. An administration marked by incompetence steadily erodes the standards Americans have long expected from their government. comments.name: Ben
comments.body:
It is sad there are 1500 deaths this year from ebola in the Congo.  

But to put it in perspective, the 2nd Congo Civil War caused 5.4 million deaths or 600,000 deaths per year, and I don't remember people being worried about that.  What if the civil war came to the USA?

More perspective...about 24,000 people die per year in the world from lightning.  Are people really worried about storms and rain? 

48,000 people die in the USA in falls.  Do we develop and wear airbag clothing to prevent death and injury in a fall?

Malaria kills 600,000 people per year and I don't lose sleep over mosquitos. 

Yet we are not talking about a lightning protection clothing (or avoiding being outside in the rain) or a civil war vaccine or wearing bullet proof vests in the Congo or covering all of our skin to avoid mosquito bites.

Constant worry about things that are very unlikely and not related to our current lives is not healthy and just causes stress which ironically makes one more likely to die as chronic stress is unhealthy.

My loved ones and I are more likely to die or be injured being shot in Chicago where we live and we don't really worry about that too much as I live here and am not ready to move or wear a bullet proof vest.  But I am not going to worry about Ebola.

But I am supposed to be worried about by dying from a disease that kills a fraction of humanity and even a fraction of people in that country compared to other causes? 

Enjoy life, relax!  and Don't Blame Trump!

comments.name: Gwen

Agreed that we can't start assembling iPhones in the US because of the labor intensity of that and the lack of added value, but there is a lot that can and should be done here.

comments.name: SVBob
comments.body:
I have been taking TRT for a couple of decades now. I was prescribed by my urologist who performed my prostatectomy. I suggested at the time that I was working just fine without it. He suggested that my muscles would thank me. 

The TRT may have helped my libido, but it is hard to tell at my age, or even 20 years ago. I have never been a violent or reactive personality, and TRT has not affected that, as far as I can tell. But, my urologist was right. My muscles thank me. Even though I am not extremely muscular, my muscle mass has remained more or less constant. Thanks, Doc.

So, I continue to rub it in.

comments.name: JV

This will certainly play out in the barracks and in the hierarchical structure of the military. Things do happen like on a few good men/ not the death but the intensity. Do they really want a much of men in close proximity that may be prone to aggression and have low inhibition? This is so stupid it would fit in the movie Idiocracy.

As a 26-year active-duty US Army Infantry veteran, serving all the way from the 1st Ranger Battalion as an NCO Squad Leader to the Deputy Battalion Commander of the largest parachute Battalion in the US Army, I can promise you we do NOT need more drugs pumped into our soldiers!
We need calm, thoughtful, experienced soldiers who are dealing with crisis situations at the ragged edge of civilization. 
We do NOT need Rambo's, John Wayne's or any of the other cartoon characters the public sees in bad war movies.

comments.body: Not that rare of a visit. Pulled in there in 2018 on the Vinson. Loved it there though. However I had to sleep on the pier as rough waters prevented us from taking the liberty boat back. Fun times.

comments.name: mike lermontov
comments.body:
I spent 22 months in the Vietnam war in 1969-1971.  The USA was on the wrong side of that conflict and everybody there at the time knew it.  Now, more than 50 years later Vietnam has become a prosperous vibrant country.  

Please Vietnam remember your history do not make any security deals with the United States, now or ever.  The United States likely thinks that Vietnam, with its long history of enmity with China, will make a fine ally in its push to dominate Asia.  Remember that the USA cannot be trusted and, if given access, will eventually turn on you and become a worse enemy than before.

comments.name: Douglas Leen
comments.body: I turn 80 in one month and participated in the first amphibious landing in the Vietnam War in 1965 at Chu Lai.  I spent my 19th and 20th birthdays on Vietnam soil.  Upon returning home, I began reading the history of this war and understood that I was fighting on the wrong side.  Three years later, I lead a student protest group which was the only group to gain access to the Oval Office (and meet with Nixon).  Twenty years later, I returned with a group of doctors as an NGO--fitting limbs on amputees.  I once learned their language.  What I admire most about the Vietnamese is that they know the art of forgiveness.  They are hard working, industrious people.  Any political and economic inroads we make with them will be in the best overall interests of both nations.

comments.name: lunasea2
comments.body: Vietnamese leadership wants it both ways.  They need and want the US for security reasons, as well as the economic considerations of its growing exports to the US.  But nothing has changed for the ideological position of its leaders.  Many Vietnamese remain very cool toward visiting Americans!

comments.name: SH
comments.body: To my dear friends who died in Vietnam, I still remember you. I will not forget. But, time moves on.

comments.name: EEngineer & Army Aviator
comments.body:
We were on the wrong side of things for the wrong reasons back then.  It's good to see that there is acceptance of the past.  I hope we continue to have better relations with the Vietnamese people.

As a comment, virtually all of the aviators I served with were multiple combat tour guys.  They had bitter feelings about the sacrifices they made and witnessed, but none of them had bad feelings towards the Vietnamese.  I was surprised then, and still am.

It's harsh, but if you want to understand Vietnam Vets, as best you can without direct experience, I suggest reading the book "The Things They Carried".

comments.name: courseV
comments.body: I had never heard of compartment syndrome until two weeks ago. A friend slipped and tumbled on a hill during a water balloon fight. The angle of the foot caused a compound fractures of both the tibia and fibula near the ankle. The EMTs felt a faint pulse and rushed her to the trauma level 1 hospital, bypassing the local hospital. She had surgery right away for compartment syndrome to reduce the swelling before  having the 4 hour surgery to put all the pins in the leg the next day.  People should be aware that it can happen even when there is no sign of external bleeding.

comments.name: jlf
comments.body: Important topic. I knew what it was from the outset, given the circumstances of a deep wound sewn up superficially.

comments.name: AB

comments.name: BB8
comments.body: We are never all going to agree, but most people I know in the Seattle area wholeheartedly agree with a change to permanent daylight savings time. We absolutely LOVE our long summer days. Switching to Standard Time would have the sun rising here at 4:45am, and closer to 4:30am in late June. NO THANKS! I don't care if it's dark till 10:00am in January, I will take more after work sunshine (than before work) any day of the week!

comments.name: OldNews
comments.body: Of course they’re opposed.  It’s a bad idea that’s been tried and failed.  People think it’s great now but they’ll sing another tune on pitch black winter mornings.

comments.name: garyinthailand
comments.body: When I relocated to Thailand in 2003, one thing that wasn't on my mind was ditching the whole 'Spring forward, Fall back' business (In the tropics, there's really no point. Daylight is nearly the same hour year-round). I was surprised to find I prefer it in that aspect. Now my only issues come up when arranging family conference calls, with participants in WA state, Arizona (year-round Standard Time) across the International Date Line. I keep having to remind my sibs that 'tomorrow 6pm' is something I have to put together with an actual date and time offset that's a moving target.

comments.name: Kevin McLaughlin
comments.body: What if we were to split the difference between daylight savings and standard time by one half hour? A little more light on both ends of the spectrum. Just enough to satisfy everyone—and annoy everyone equally.

comments.name: Oxfdblue
comments.body:
Why does it seem that no one, even people old enough to actually remember it forget that we tried this year-round daylight savings time thing in 1973.  It was supposed to be a two-year trial. It failed so spectacularly and was so unpopular (not mention, dangerous) that it was canceled after one year.
I clearly remember being an 11-year-old standing out in the dark waiting for a school bus and the sun not coming up until we were over an hour into the school day. It was absolutely horrendous. I feel that people have lost all sense of history and all sense of memory. We’re going to repeat the same ridiculous experiment we tried 53 years ago with the same ridiculously poor results.

comments.name: ManhattanWilliam
comments.body: Orthodox Jews are opposed, and some farmers?  Too bad, a large majority of Americans don't want it and in this case the majority is correct.  Time for it to go.

articles.title: Not Everyone Wants Year-Round Daylight Saving Time
articles.summary: Some Orthodox Jews oppose a bill that would make daylight saving time permanent, and farmers and some sleep experts are also opposed.

comments.name: mark
comments.body: Obviously there is no reason to believe any information being put out by the U.S. military.

comments.name: Michael Cassidy
comments.body: I'm quite curious as to why it is the Times' apparent policy to essentially always uncritically and blithely repeat that any and all Iranian missle and drone attacks were intercepted and did no or nominal damage, as always noncredibly claimed by US Central Command and its Gulf allies. It is patently absurd and quite obviously untrue that Iran is not causing significant damage and harm. It has been demonstrated elsewhere, and even once in these pages a month ago after obtaining satellite images, that Iran's reporting of damage it has inflicted has been accurate. The reality is that the US bases and assets throughout the region have been devastated, causing the US to retreat to Jordan, quarter troops in hotels and other off-base locations, and continue to stage its carriers and fleet far away from Iran's reach. The US increasingly retreating from Jordan as well. So, why not at least report Iran's accounts of the damage and impacts they assert their attacks have caused, in the same manner you dutifully report the claims of the US and its allies that Iran's attacks are almost always  ineffectual? Clearly, US military is losing this illegal war of aggression. The longer this paper continues to only report the US and its allies' obvious lies about its military losses, the longer this coverage enables them to distort the reality that they have lost. The longer this happens, the longer Trump can prolong his unwillingness to concede defeat and seek real peace with Iran.

comments.name: don healy
comments.body: The reports of governments in the Middle East led by autocratic rulers with prohibitions on free speech cannot be trusted with their claims that they are shooting down Iranian drones and missiles without suffering damage, injuries or deaths. Likewise, the US  DOD has shown that they cannot be trusted to be honest.

comments.name: Hamilton Federalist
comments.body:
So Iran struck a Jordanian base, killed and wounded US soldiers AND at least one F-35 but total silence by the Department of Defense? Even later the US updating the wounded and killed exponentially?  Pathetic. So now Kuwait has better defenses than a US base? Exactly---total fiction. If you simply place US war rhetoric next to such facts of this wacky war Hegseth's and Trump's lies are readily apparent. 

Declare victory and send our poor troops home. Marines and sailors afloat for nearly half a year?!  All for Israel's imperialism and the influence of the US billionaires who dangle donations before Trump? Sad indeed.

comments.name: Lillas Pasta
comments.body: Am I alone in seeing a strange reverse echo between the current war involving Iran against Israel and the U.S., and the opening stages of the Second World War?  Like the U.S.'s position throughout late 1939, all of 1940, and most of 1941, Europe's territorial integrity and security hasn't been directly threatened by a war taking place a long way away at the far end of the Persian Gulf, in which a Western power is engaged in military conflict with an authoritarian, extremist regime that has vowed to eradicate a Jewish state and its population, while at the same time inflicting massive harm on its own people who have repeatedly protested against their government (Kristallnacht?).  So, as the U.S. sat out the first two-plus years of the European and Pacific conflict from September, 1939 until December, 1941, Western Europe is sitting out the war that pits Iran against the U.S. and Israel (and increasingly other countries in the region -- Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain, Jordan, and now even Egypt).  But just as Pearl Harbor compelled the U.S. to enter WWII, so eventually the Iranian overreach in attempting to starve the rest of the world from having access to oil may compel the Western Europe nations to join the coalition against Iran in order to protect themselves.

comments.name: PR
comments.body: Can we actually believe this administration's assertions about casualties and damage to U.S. military and assets?  Hourly deceptions and flip flops about many topics, both serious and goofy, suggest NO.  I don't mean they never give truthful information, but  it is so often self-serving, misleading and contradictory that it is near worthless.  Sad but true.

comments.name: How to negotiate 101
comments.body:
The U.S. military says there was “no major impact” on U.S. bases… so there was minor impact?

The lack of information from the Pentagon has backfired. Hegseth prevented any embedded reporters with troops to control information. But the result has been zero stories on deployed soldiers - they are nameless and faceless. Remember the aviator who was rescued at great cost after being shot down in Iran? That person was never identified or publicly interviewed. What about the repairs to the U.S.S. Gerald Ford that had a “laundry room fire”? No stories on that.  Hegseth has prevented the U.S. public from identifying with its soldiers, who remain anonymous numbers.

comments.name: Chris McClure
comments.body: It is unfortunate but true that we have run out of valuable military targets to strike in Iran. All of their remaining leaders and weaponry are now so well hidden that it would take the wholesale destruction of the country to neutralize the threat. The regime lives on and earlier penetration by Israeli intelligence has run its course. We have an array of bad options to choose from, and clearly we have not achieved most of our objectives. The Trump administration should have framed this conflict as a liberation for the Persian people instead of an ill-defined war of destruction planned by Israeli leadership. We had a golden opportunity and lost it because we didn’t include our experts in the planning. Trump will be remembered as the greatest failure in American history. We have let the Persians and the entire region down in a big way. Trump should resign immediately for his inexcusable failure as the commander in chief.

comments.name: Free
comments.body:

comments.name: Tri State
comments.body: I didn’t know Simone Forti but I knew of her and her influence on the post-modern Judson Church and Grand Union choreographers from the 1960s. I danced with one of them, David Gordon and his wife Valda in their dance group. We created and performed pieces that combined speaking and movement. We are reaching the end of an era of those special artists.

comments.name: Liz Christo
comments.body: I will never forget her workshops in the 90s. Improvising moving and talking simultaneously with her was like magic. She always made the most simple moments feel profound almost out of thin air. I'm so grateful for her gentle, awake presence. Indeed one of the most beautiful people I have ever known.

comments.name: Sally

comments.name: Tim Wolf
comments.body: Simone Forti's "Handbook in Motion" was a real inspiration for me as a young artist in the 70s and 80s. She and her work guided and inspired me as I explored improvisational forms in music and dance. I was fortunate to see her perform on a few occasions and meet with her in her loft on lower Broadway. Thank you, Simone.

comments.name: Sarah Swenson

Beyond New York, she spent the last 28 years a highly visible and generous contributor to the Los Angeles dance community, teaching and creating all kinds of art, but especially performance work, most recently curating an evening at Highways Performance  Space, Santa Monica, November 2024, in which she also performed at the age of 89.

They were always entertaining, funny as hell and did a good job of alienating as many people as possible. They always seemed to have a higher energy when performing in Golden Gate Park as well as my college, San Francisco State. Bruce Barthol, from Country Joe and the Fish, was the honcho for some years after Davis. Actually for a long time. It was time when people aren't afraid-like now-to express themselves. It would be a real treat if Ronnie Davis could come back in some form and do what he did; make people feel alive while stating the rampant injustice in society.He was real special guy in a time that had lots of special guys and women.

comments.name: Keith R.

The obit leaves a fair amount out, with no mention of the Troupe’s ribald adaptation of Alfred Jarry’s “Ubu Roi”, with musical additions by Steve Reich, which was performed outdoors, and in its performance space in a former church in the Mission district. R.G. was also an extraordinarily talented mime who performed solo works by Samuel Becket, his “Act II Without Words”  notably among them, in the Actors Workshop’s smaller, more intimate theater in S.F. Perhaps that’s brought up in his book, along with mention of some his troupe’s memorable performers, Victoria Hochberg, as Mere Ubu, among them.  

Ronnie deserves a biography that covers his important contribution to street theater and freedom of speech, as well as remembering his brilliant, sometimes caustic, sometimes sweet, and often sharply witty personality.

comments.name: Muleshoe2
comments.body:
Thank you Max, for a wonderful piece of reporting. Your description of the DC-3 coupled with stories of the people who trust her to supply their daily lives was joyful. Every line and photograph moved me or jogged a memory.

Your article touched on three cornerstones of my own life. I am 72 and consider myself fortunate to “never have had a career,” as the spouse of one friend remarked. I worked in a variety of occupations that allowed me to work on the City Desk at the Dallas Morning News out of college, travel extensively in South America for an American equipment manufacturer and I always have had a love of planes. 

A Cessna Skymaster, a unique “push-me pull-you” two-engine plane flew at low altitude every week over an oil pipeline that crossed our farm in western Oklahoma. As a very young kid I used to wave to the pilot and yearn for a chance to fly and see the world as he did. 

I’m a plane nerd of many years. The twin-boomed  Skymaster made me a sucker for the P-38 Lightning. I began my quest for a pilots license in the late ‘70’s under Edna Garner Whyte, age 74 at the time, a pioneer and accomplished female pilot. 

I have not piloted a plane in many years but the roar of an engine above still draws my eye skyward. 

Thanks again for starting my day off with tons of great memories. I hope journalism continues to offer you great memories of your own. I’ll watch for more of your work.

I grew up seeing more than a few “Dakota”s and had an Uncle who flew them into desolate Yemen and Ethiopia in the 70”s and into the early 80’s ..(having retired from Indian Air Force, Hurricanes, Ouragons, Vampires, and Canberra (the US version was the Martin B57) …for the fly boys of that era and for a few today. This was real flying, all instruments, steady hands , risk taking and luck…great writing that captured the essence of this spirit

As a teen I flew to Guatemala on DC-4’s to Guatemala to visit my father, who flew Stearman’s there as a crop duster. Flying in these vintage aircraft was a visceral experience I’ll never forget. To this day I’m still a stick and rudder pilot.

We saw an article in Flying magazine about a small airline flying a Grumman Goose on a schedule from Long Beach to Catalina. We took a detour, rode in the Goose to Catalina and back. comments.name: Gandalf the Blue
comments.body:
I was skeptical about bringing "Harry Potter" to the stage, especially after reading the published script for "Cursed Child," which seemed more appropriate for a film, given some of the nonrealistic scenes, but the creative team pulled it off.

I saw "HP&TCC" before the 2 halves were combined into 1 shorter play during Covid, & it was truly spectacular.

There is no reason why a GOT-based mega-play couldn't work onstage since, as the article pointed out, GRRM based much of his series on Shakespeare's history plays & tragedies.

But it does take a huge investment of cash & a great deal of commitment from cast, crew, designers, &--ultimately--audiences. (I can't imagine a ticket for the play will be cheap, even with the U.K.'s subsidy of RSC & theatre in general.)

I look forward to reading the reviews when it finally opens, & I wish them all the luck in the world. 

Despite lots of gratuitous violence/gore & sex/nudity, I'm a GOT fan because it's a great story with interesting characters & amazing production values.

House of the Dragons hasn't been at the same level as GOT, except in some aspects (excellence of F/X to create believable dragons, for example).

And I enjoyed A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms quite a bit, even with its narrower focus, smaller scale. (Still dislike the gratuitous nudity & gore.)

We can't make mythology out of contemporary reality, but there are plenty of relevant lessons in these fantasy series or single works (e.g., Nolan's "The Odyssey").

comments.name: Kiwi Rick
comments.body:
Agree wholeheartedly with Heather from San Diego, but on an individual level all of us need to become climate warriors.   Taking our long-haul flights for holidays and then smugly shaking our heads at the climate deniers reflects our own inability to accept the inconvenient truths that Al Gore presented to us 20 years ago.    Here are some things all of us can do on an individual level:
* Convert all internal combustion engines in your life to electric -- this moves you to a good place and pushes the marketplace.   Also, your neighbors will notice and you may nudge them to do the right thing
* Mow less lawn; regenerate
* Pay a reasonable amount to cover air travel into one of the many carbon offset funds available.  This amount should be part of your travel budget.  
* Solar panels/batteries on every house (or where feasible)
* Air dry your clothes like grandma used to do -- they smell great and will last longer (dryers beat up clothing -- what do you think lint is?)
* share the word..... gently.

This is truly heart breaking – we live not far and Dunwich is one of our favourite walking places. And RSPB Minsmere one of the jewels of conservation.  This time of year it would be blooming with purple heather and yellow gorse and glorious with bird song and butterfly wings, and the sound of North Sea waves .  I wish I could share a photo of its previous beauty. 

Suffolk firefighters are doing a sterling job with reinforcements from around the country. We pray they all stay safe.
This has always been one of the driest places in the UK but still a temperate place. But never have we known such drought conditions as these.  No real rain since the end of March – a parched April and May, a little rain at the beginning of June and none since. And four heatwaves.

 The ground is like rock and our crops cemented into the ground and not harvestable. Stock eating winter feed, cereal yields are 20% down , in some cases much more. 
 
We don’t need convincing about climate change here.

Please US - do try to convince your President.

We have had next to no rain for two months, temperatures well above 25C most of the time, often on their 30s. Everywhere is fragile and scorched. 

The fire crews are doing a tremendous job confining it for the moment as the countryside around here is a tinderbox

He or she would set an example and do the following:

•	Increase the budget of the EPA and expand the Office of Climate Adaptation and Sustainability.
•	Maintain subsidies for solar energy and EV charging stations.
•	Increase funding for public transportation.
•	Set up a green challenge initiative to encourage cities to build sustainable infrastructure.
•	Allow Chinese car companies to sell their small EV cars to the U.S.—and encourage U.S. car makers to build similar, competitive models.
•	Increase funding for diplomatic cooperation to decrease wars-of-choice.
•	Emphasize the message that united we stand, divided we fall applies to all nations on Earth when it comes to building a more sustainable future.
•	Set up global training and resource sharing to fight wildfires and desertification. 
•	Create subsidies and incentives for private companies to develop carbon removal technologies.

I can dream, can’t I?

“Are there any other democracies that still has (sic) the death penalty?” 

“Yes, but it’s extremely rare.”

comments.name: Mandibular
comments.body:
U.S. citizen here.

I have very little sympathy with Richard Allen Davis, John William King, Lawrence Russell Brewer, and Shawn Allen Berry.  And I do not lose a lot of sleep over Timothy McVeigh.

But the christianist  justification of "Biblical retribution"?  Let's look at this.

1. "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth" was an improvement (if you will) at the time.  It was no longer a leg for a tooth or a life for an eye.  It was the maximum punishment that could not be extracted, not the standard for all time.

2. Again, concerning an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, and by extension a life for a life, we have a system of criminal and civil penalty that we apply.  We do not sentence sexual assaulters to be assaulted or sentence a litterbug to have trash dumped on his lawn.

3. But the biggest hole in the christianist justification for the death penalty: it may be safe to conjecture that (to use the example above) Richard Allen Davis has not accepted Christ as savior and lord.  By executing him, you sentence him to eternal punishment.  As long as he is alive, he may be saved.  Or?  

(By this argument, I suppose that it was OK for George Bush Jr. to execute Karla Faye Tucker, who spent 14 years on death row, during which she underwent a profound religious conversion to Christianity.  But let's not go down there.)

comments.name: Jay E. Simkin
comments.body:
"America is a place where violence leads to death more often because of the prevalence of guns."

Not so!! The idea that firearms promote violence is error. New Hampshire (NH) has few laws as to firearms. At least since 2001 - save for 2015 -  it has been among the three safest states, measured by the incidence of violence crime per 100,000 residents. Data sources: FBI Crime Data Explorer and Bureau of Justice Statistics. 

Since 2013, the incidence of violent crime in New Hampshire (NH) has halved, from 223.2/100,000 residents to 111.0/100,000 residents (2024). Yet, in 2017, NH ended compulsory licensur for concealed carry of firearms.  The incidence of violent crime dinimished even during the COVID pandemic!!

By contrast, from 1985 through 2024, Massachusetts (MA) - with thickets of nasty and repressive laws as to firearms - has had not less than 1.8 times the incidence of violent crimes, realtive to NH. 

Nationally, the incidence of violence crime fell from a post-1960 peak of 758.2 per 100,000 (1992) to 370.8 (2024). Yet, during that time, the number of firearms in the U.S. rose from 217 million  to 511 million (in 2023; data published by US Departments of Treasury and Justice). 

In short, it is error to claim that firearm availability promotes violent crime  

Also clear: "gun control" laws keep repressive - indeed murderous - rêgimes in power. Iran's clerico-military rêgime has murdered thousands of unarmed protesters. Yet, no one will help Iranians by arming them.

comments.name: Liemba
comments.body:
I am not sure if I fully agree with the way the South Korean stock market’s recent performance is described. Personally, I highly doubt that it was the retail investors causing these volatile fluctuations on their own, nor do I think foreign investors are returning as if they had left in the first place.

If I am not mistaken, the KOSPI is heavily influenced and massively owned by foreign institutional investors. To monitor their profound influence, I believe the South Korean stock market even built a dedicated tracking category for foreign investor activities.

Based on my observation, I tend to believe that these fluctuations were likely driven by algorithmic triggers and opportunistic trading activities by institutional traders. Many retail investors likely involuntarily got either stopped out or closed out of their margin positions, triggering cascading effects and causing the share prices to go lower by the time hedge fund managers and institutional traders subsequently stepped in to readjust their positions. At least, that’s my view.

I’ve lived in Europe for 50 years. For a long time authorities across Europe have walked on eggshells where supporters of Islamic movements & antisemitism were concerned, afraid of being called “racist” and losing political/partisan support. The  recent decades of massive increase in immigration from some countries & attacks on civilians, especially Jews, have played a role as well. 

I sense a reckoning change happening at several levels across Europe. Beginning with the most recent “EU Migration Pact”. Many new controls (biometric databases) & better communications between countries with see easier control, tracking & deportation of migrants who break laws or pose a threat to national security. 

Even Spain has called in their army and border nations have increased border controls to respond to the tens of thousands trying to enter Europe via Ceuta  unchecked.
